text: To better match the empirical data, ResStock uses an increased thermal capacitance multiplier for the air inside the dwelling units. If the root cause is an underestimate of the thermal mass, the results could also underestimate the amount of time required to effectively preheat or precool the dwellings. The models used in ResStock represent the building stock circa 2018 using weather from 2018, but the goal is to estimate the potential of demand flexibility in 2050. Based on the slow speed of retrofits in the building stock and the slow uptake of envelope upgrades, the use of today’s building stock is believed to be an acceptable limitation. The impact of not using future weather projections is more difficult to assess. On one hand, average temperatures are not expected to change dramatically by 2050. On the other hand, extreme temperatures, which might or might not be coincident with the peak periods, could change more dramatically. This measure relies on the inputs for on-peak hours during summer, winter and intermediate seasons. We selected a grid peak load reduction approach for the year 2050 as the target of this study. This could create higher customer costs or grid operation costs, depending on the utility rate design and other factors. The choice of future load scenario in Cambium and the fact that the future load profile does not include wide-scale electrification could also significantly impact the timing of the peak periods. An analysis of these factors would require modeling the future power system, including the dispatch of demand response resources. That modeling is beyond the scope of this analysis. Finally, the choice of pre-peak and on-peak durations and the set point offset are applied uniformly across the entire building stock; however, optimal settings likely vary, depending on the climate and the building’s characteristics. For example, a long pre-peak duration might not be effective for dwellings with poor exterior insulation because they tend to lose heat quickly. 4.7 Future Work The results provided in this analysis could be expanded in several ways. First, determining the peak period windows for targeting the load reduction could be based on different future load profiles—in particular, load profiles assuming major electrification of vehicles and space heating. If those load profiles significantly shift the timing of the peak load window, performing new analysis might be warranted. If the timing of the windows shifts only minimally, the uncertainty due to other future changes might outweigh the uncertainty in these results. Second, these results could be recreated using a future building stock. In 2050, some dwellings that exist in today’s ResStock model will have been demolished, whereas others will have been retrofitted with new equipment, and new dwellings will have been built. All these changes could impact the results.
